newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola fighting intensifies, civilians flee.
newsitem.headline: Angola fighting intensifies, civilians flee.

text.p: Clashes between the Angolan government and UNITA fighters have intensified and thousands of civilians have fled from villages in the northeast of the country, aid workers said on Thursday.
The clashes are the biggest since the rivals signed a ceasefire in 1994 and have triggered fears of a return to war.
Relief agency staff told Reuters thousands of villagers had fled to the safety of the government-controlled Nzage diamond mining town to escape fierce battles.
The aid workers also quoted villagers as saying many civilians had been killed in three weeks of clashes between government forces and UNITA fighters.
The government claimed it launched the offensive to get rid of armed refugees who crossed into Angola after the fall of Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko.
But observers say that was just a pretext for a renewed attempt to recapture rich diamond fields still under UNITA control despite a peace agreement and a government of national unity.

"The number of internally displaced are being registered and the figure is at around 3,500. We've been told to expect more because of fighting," a U.N. relief official told Reuters after returning from a visit to the region this week.
"The people coming into Nzage saying the war has started again and civilians are being killed."
Relief workers said they saw about 70 wounded government troops being treated at a local hospital, but there was no word on UNITA casualties.
Mining officials in the town said government troops were patrolling the main road between Nzage and the northern border town of Dundo and have ordered civilians to keep out of the area.

Mining sources said there had been many refugees from the forme Zaire outside Nzage, but Angolan troops had stripped them of their possessions and driven them back towards the border with their old homeland, about 70 km (44 miles) to the east.

Philip Sibanda, commander of the U.N. force overseeing the Angolan peace process, said this week after a visit to the area he had seen evidence of fighting. He estimated that at least 14 government soldiers had been killed and 90 wounded.

On Tuesday, the government and UNITA convened a national unity parliament. But analysts said there was a major gap between UNITA's representatives in the Luanda legislature and party leader Jonas Savimbi and his generals.
They have refused to go the capital and remain at their bush headquarters despite the peace process meant to end two decades of civil war that broke out after independence from Portugal in 1975.
